claim: Adenylate cyclases convert intra- and extracellular stimuli into a second messenger cAMP signal.
source: Adenylate cyclases convert intra- and extracellular stimuli into a second messenger cAMP signal.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of adenylate cyclases.

claim: Many bacterial and most eukaryotic ACs possess membrane anchors with six transmembrane spans.
source: Many bacterial and most eukaryotic ACs possess membrane anchors with six transmembrane spans.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: The membrane anchor of AC Rv1625c can be replaced by the quorum-sensing receptor from Vibrio harveyi to obtain an active, membrane-anchored AC.
source: We replaced the anchor of the AC Rv1625c by the quorum-sensing receptor from Vibrio harveyi which has an identical 6TM design and obtained an active, membrane-anchored AC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing AC activity in the chimera construct.

claim: A canonical class III AC is ligand-regulated in vitro and in vivo.
source: We show that a canonical class III AC is ligand-regulated in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from AC assays and in vivo E. coli experiments.

claim: At 10 µM, the cholera-autoinducer CAI-1 stimulates AC activity 4.8-fold.
source: At 10 µM, the cholera-autoinducer CAI-1 stimulates activity 4.8-fold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from AC activity assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: Sequence-based clustering of membrane domains of class III ACs and quorum-sensing receptors established six groups of potential structural and functional similarities.
source: A sequence based clustering of membrane domains of class III ACs and quorum-sensing receptors established six groups of potential structural and functional similarities.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis presented in Figure 7.

claim: 6TM AC membrane domains may operate as receptors which directly regulate AC activity.
source: The data support the notion that 6TM AC membrane domains may operate as receptors which directly regulate AC activity as opposed and in addition to the indirect regulation by GPCRs in eukaryotic congeners.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing direct ligand regulation of the chimeric AC.

claim: In 1958 Sutherland and Rall reported the structure of cAMP as a second messenger.
source: In 1958 Sutherland and Rall reported the structure of a second messenger, cyclic 3',5'-adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) which was generated upon incubation of a liver extract with the first messengers epinephrine or glucagon (Sutherland and Rall, 1958).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sutherland and Rall, 1958.

claim: cAMP has been demonstrated to be a universal second messenger translating a variety of extracellular stimuli into a uniform intracellular chemical signal.
source: Since then cAMP has been demonstrated to be a universal second messenger translating a variety of extracellular stimuli into a uniform intracellular chemical signal.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by extensive literature.

claim: Adenylate cyclases have been biochemically and genetically identified in most bacterial and eukaryotic cells.
source: The enzymes responsible for biosynthesis of cAMP from ATP, adenylate cyclases (ACs), have been biochemically and genetically identified in most bacterial and eukaryotic cells (Khandelwal and Hamilton, 1971; Linder and Schultz, 2003; 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Khandelwal and Hamilton, 1971; Linder and Schultz, 2003; 2008.

claim: Sequencing has identified six classes of ACs.
source: To date, sequencing has identified six classes of ACs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from AC classification literature.

claim: Class I, II, and minor classes IV-VI ACs are restricted to bacteria.
source: The small-sized class I (enterobacterial ACs), class II (toxin class) and the minor classes IV-VI are restricted to bacteria (Bârzu and Danchin, 1994; Linder and Schultz, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bârzu and Danchin, 1994; Linder and Schultz, 2003.

claim: Class III ACs are ubiquitous, albeit with differing domain architectures.
source: The class III ACs are ubiquitous, albeit with differing domain architectures (Linder and Schultz, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Linder and Schultz, 2008.

claim: The catalytic domains of ACs share sequence and structural similarities.
source: The catalytic domains share sequence and structural similarities, yet minor, characteristic sequence peculiarities have resulted in a division into four subclasses, a-d (Linder and Schultz, 2008; Tesmer et al., 1997; Tews et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Linder and Schultz, 2008; Tesmer et al., 1997; Tews et al., 2005.

claim: Bacterial ACs are monomers which require homodimerization for activity.
source: A fundamental difference between bacterial and eukaryotic ACs is that the former are monomers which require homodimerization for activity.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial AC structure and function.

claim: Mammalian ACs are pseudoheterodimers composed of two concatenated 'bacterial' monomers with slightly diverged, yet complementary domains.
source: The mammalian congeners, exclusively class IIIa, present themselves as pseudoheterodimers composed of two concatenated 'bacterial' monomers with slightly diverged, yet complementary domains (Guo et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2001.

claim: Mammalian class III ACs are anchored to the membrane by two putative 6TM bundles, one in each of the concatenated repeats.
source: Accordingly, mammalian class III ACs are anchored to the membrane by two putative 6TM bundles, one in each of the concatenated repeats.
evidence: This is based on inference from the pseudoheterodimeric structure of mammalian ACs.

claim: Knowledge about regulation of bacterial class III ACs is limited.
source: Our knowledge about regulation of bacterial class III ACs is limited.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: A few soluble ACs appear to be regulated by carbon dioxide or pH.
source: Apart from a few soluble ACs which appear to be regulated by carbon dioxide or pH near to nothing is known (Kleinboelting et al., 2014; Steegborn et al., 2005; Tews et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kleinboelting et al., 2014; Steegborn et al., 2005; Tews et al., 2005.

claim: The established regulation of the nine mammalian, membrane-delimited AC isoforms is indirect.
source: The established regulation of the nine mammalian, membrane-delimited AC isoforms is indirect.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mammalian AC regulation.

claim: Stimulation of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) by extracellular ligands releases Gsα intracellularly which binds to ACs and activates.
source: Stimulation of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) by extracellular ligands releases Gsα intracellularly which binds to ACs and activates.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about GPCR-mediated AC regulation.

claim: A potentially direct ligand-regulation of class III ACs via their large membrane anchors remains a genuine possibility.
source: A potentially direct ligand-regulation of class III ACs via their large membrane anchors remains a genuine possibility.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural features of AC membrane anchors.

claim: The 6TM membrane anchors of bacterial ACs are structural analogs of the 6TM bundles in mammalian ACs.
source: The 6TM membrane anchors of bacterial ACs are obviously structural analogs of the 6TM bundles in mammalian ACs.
evidence: This is based on inference from structural similarities between bacterial and mammalian AC membrane domains.

claim: The membrane anchor of the mycobacterial AC Rv3645 was replaced by the E. coli chemotaxis receptors for serine (Tsr) and aspartate (Tar).
source: In the past, we replaced the membrane anchor of the mycobacterial AC Rv3645 by the E. coli chemotaxis receptors for serine, Tsr, and aspartate, Tar (Kanchan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kanchan et al., 2010.

claim: Tsr/Tar and Rv3645 have a signal-transducing HAMP domain in common and both require dimerization.
source: Tsr/Tar and Rv3645 have a signal-transducing HAMP domain in common and both require dimerization.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about these proteins.

claim: Tsr/Tar-Rv3645 chimeras were regulated in vitro and in vivo by serine or aspartate.
source: The chimeras were regulated in vitro and in vivo by serine or aspartate (Kanchan et al., 2010; Mondéjar et al., 2012; Winkler et al., 2012), i.e. a 2TM receptor, Tsr or Tar, with an extensive periplasmic ligand-binding domain replaced a 6TM AC membrane anchor which lacks periplasmic loops.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kanchan et al., 2010; Mondéjar et al., 2012; Winkler et al., 2012.

claim: Direct regulation of a class III AC via an extracellular ligand is a possibility.
source: The data demonstrated that in principle direct regulation of a class III AC via an extracellular ligand is a possibility.
evidence: This is based on inference from the Tsr/Tar-Rv3645 chimera experiments.

claim: Membrane anchors with 6TMs are present in many proteins.
source: Membrane anchors with 6TMs are present in many proteins.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about protein membrane domains.

claim: 6TM membrane anchors often have short transmembrane-spanning α-helices and short connecting loops.
source: Often they have short transmembrane-spanning α-helices and short connecting loops, e.g. in bacterial and mammalian ACs (Krupinski et al., 1989; Linder and Schultz, 2003), in the cytochrome subunits of succinate dehydrogenases and fumarate reductases (Hederstedt, 1998; Yankovskaya et al., 2003), ABC transporters (Chang and Roth, 2001), in bacterial HdeD proteins (Mates et al., 2007), six transmembrane epithelial antigen of the prostate (STEAP, Kleven et al., 2015), or quorum-sensing (QS) receptors from Vibrio and Legionella which have His-kinases as cytosolic effectors (Ng and Bassler, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: Lipophilic ligands have been identified for quorum-sensing receptors from Vibrio and Legionella.
source: For the latter lipophilic ligands have been identified (Ng et al., 2011; 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ng et al., 2011; 2010.

claim: Rv1625c is considered to be an ancestral form of mammalian ACs.
source: We chose the mycobacterial class IIIa AC Rv1625c for this investigation because of its similarity to the mammalian congeners (Guo et al., 2001) and the QS-receptor from V. harveyi.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2001.

claim: Both Rv1625c and CqsS require dimerization to be catalytically active.
source: Both proteins require dimerization to be catalytically active.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The success of generating a functionally productive chimera between the AC and the QS-receptor hinges on finding a suitable point of transition between both proteins.
source: The success of generating a functionally productive chimera between the AC and the QS-receptor hinges on the precondition that a suitable point of transition between both proteins can be found which allows signal propagation from the CqsS receptor to the AC effector.
evidence: This is based on inference from protein engineering principles.

claim: 15 different points of connection between the CqsS receptor and the catalytic domain of Rv1625c were probed.
source: Therefore, 15 different points of connection between the CqsS receptor and the catalytic domain of Rv1625c were probed.
evidence: This is experimental data describing the approach taken.

claim: The chimera CqsS1-168Rv1625c203-443 was active (16.2 nmol cAMP·mg-1·min-1), but unregulated.
source: The chimera CqsS1-168Rv1625c203-443 was active (16.2 nmol cAMP·mg-1·min-1), but unregulated.
evidence: This is experimental data from AC activity assays.

claim: The basal AC activity of the CqsS1-168Rv1625c203-443 chimera was comparable to that of the membrane-bound Rv1625c holoenzyme.
source: The basal AC activity of this chimera was comparable to that of the membrane-bound Rv1625c holoenzyme (Guo et al., 2001), i.e. generally the two disparate domains were functionally fully compatible with each other.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data with cited literature.

claim: In the cyanobacterial class IIIa AC CyaG from Arthrospira platensis a distinct N-terminal domain that starts with RSEELL was required for a functional interaction with the chemotaxis receptor Tsr.
source: In the cyanobacterial class IIIa AC CyaG from Arthrospira platensis a distinct N-terminal domain that starts with RSEELL, was required for a functional interaction with the chemotaxis receptor Tsr (Winkler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Winkler et al., 2012.

claim: A comparison between CyaG and Rv1625c AC sequences revealed a similar domain in Rv1625c beginning with RSEALL.
source: A comparison between CyaG and Rv1625c AC sequences revealed a similar domain in Rv1625c beginning with RSEALL (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 1.

claim: The auto-phosphorylated histidine in the CqsS His-kinase is part of the canonical H-box.
source: In the CqsS His-kinase the auto-phosphorylated histidine is part of the canonical H-box (underlined in Figure 1; Grebe and Stock, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grebe and Stock, 1999 and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Several chimeras of CqsS and Rv1625c linked in the H-box region were unaffected by CAI-1.
source: However, several chimeras of CqsS and Rv1625c linked in this region were unaffected by CAI-1.
evidence: This is experimental data from AC activity assays.

claim: With transition points closer to the membrane exit of the CqsS receptor (e.g. at Val172, Ala181 or Gly185), AC activities were reproducibly stimulated by CAI-1.
source: With transition points closer to the membrane exit of the CqsS receptor, e.g. at Val172, Ala181 or Gly185, AC activities were reproducibly stimulated by CAI-1 (not shown).
evidence: This is experimental data from AC activity assays.

claim: The chimera CqsS1-181-Rv1625c218-443 responded maximally to CAI-1.
source: For further experiments we linked Ala181 of the QS-receptor to Arg218 of the Rv1625c AC, generating CqsS1-181-Rv1625c218-443 (abbreviated CqsS-Rv1625c; Figure 1) because it responded maximally.
evidence: This is experimental data from AC activity assays.

claim: The chimera CqsS-Rv1625c was stimulated by 85% with 10 µM CAI-1.
source: The chimera CqsS-Rv1625c was stimulated by 85% with 10 µM CAI-1 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The response of CqsS-Rv1625c to CAI-1 was concentration-dependent.
source: The response was concentration-dependent and the EC50 concentration for CAI-1 was 400 nM (Figure 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The EC50 concentration for CAI-1 stimulation of CqsS-Rv1625c was 400 nM.
source: The response was concentration-dependent and the EC50 concentration for CAI-1 was 400 nM (Figure 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Discrimination between CAI-1 with a C9 and LAI-1 with a C11 lipid tail was absent in CqsS-Rv1625c.
source: Discrimination between CAI-1 with a C9 and LAI-1 with a C11 lipid tail was absent. In both cases maximal stimulation at 10 µM CAI-1 and the EC50 concentrations were identical (Figure 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The EC50 concentration of 400 nM for CAI-1 in the CqsS-Rv1625c chimera perfectly matched the concentrations required to observe phenotypic responses from the CqsS-His-kinase in V. cholerae.
source: These parameters perfectly matched the concentrations of 400 nM required to observe phenotypic responses from the CqsS-His-kinase in V. cholerae (Ng et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on comparison with data from cited literature.

claim: In vivo characterization of CqsS from V. cholerae identified Cys170 at the exit of TM6 as critical for signaling.
source: In vivo characterization of CqsS from V. cholerae identified Cys170 at the exit of TM6 as critical for signaling (Ng et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ng et al., 2011.

claim: In CqsS from V. harveyi the residue corresponding to Cys170 in V. cholerae CqsS is Phe166.
source: In CqsS from V. harveyi the corresponding residue is Phe166 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 1.

claim: Substitutions of Phe166 by large flexible hydrophobic residues (Leu, Ile, or Met) enhanced CAI-1 stimulation up to 480% compared to 185% with the parent Phe166 construct.
source: Substitutions by large flexible hydrophobic residues, i.e. Leu, Ile, or Met enhanced CAI-1 stimulation up to 480% compared to 185% with the parent Phe166 construct (compare Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The F166L substitution in CqsS effectuated high discrimination between CAI-1 and LAI-1, with the potency ratio CAI-1/LAI-1 at 10 µM increasing from 1 to 3.
source: Furthermore, a high discrimination between CAI-1 and LAI-1 was effectuated and the potency ratio CAI-1/LAI-1 at 10 µM increased from 1 to 3 (see Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The F166L CqsS sensor domain in the chimera shows high selectivity between CAI-1 and LAI-1.
source: Evidently, the F166L CqsS sensor domain in the chimera shows high selectivity between CAI-1 and LAI-1.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing differential responses to CAI-1 and LAI-1.

claim: The natural CqsS receptor preferably detects ligands with C10 or C8 but not shorter (C6, C4) or longer (C12, e.g. LAI-1) alkyl tails.
source: Our findings were in line with earlier results that the natural CqsS receptor preferably detects ligands with C10 or C8 but not shorter (C6, C4) or longer (C12, e.g. LAI-1) alkyl tails (Tiaden and Hilbi, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tiaden and Hilbi, 2012.

claim: 3,4-tridecanediol stimulated AC activity by about 10% of CAI-1 at 10 μM.
source: 3, 4-tridecanediol which has not been reported as a natural ligand stimulated by about 10% of CAI-1 at 10 μM (Figure 3).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Tryptophan substitution at position 166 of CqsS abrogated CAI-1 stimulation.
source: Other amino acid substitutions at position 166 of CqsS did not affect the extent of AC stimulation with the exception of tryptophan which abrogated stimulation (data not shown).
evidence: This is experimental data from AC activity assays.

claim: CAI-1 activation enhanced Vmax from 14 to 42 nmol cAMP·mg-1·min-1 whereas Km for substrate ATP was not significantly affected (233 and 163 µM ATP, respectively).
source: Activation enhanced Vmax from 14 to 42 nmol cAMP·mg-1·min-1 whereas Km for substrate ATP was not significantly affected (233 and 163 µM ATP, respectively).
evidence: This is experimental data from kinetic analysis of AC activity.

claim: An up to 104-fold activation of CqsS-stimulated reporter gene transcription was earlier observed in V. harveyi and V. cholerae.
source: An up to 104-fold activation of CqsS-stimulated reporter gene transcription was earlier observed in V. harveyi and V. cholerae (21).
evidence: This is supported by citation (reference 21 in the text).

claim: The 5-fold activation of CqsS-F166L reported in this study appears comparatively small compared to the 104-fold activation in reporter gene studies.
source: The 5-fold activation of CqsS-F166L reported here appears comparatively small.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data with cited literature.

claim: The discrepancy in activation levels can be explained by the fact that the amplification systems used differ profoundly.
source: This discrepancy can be explained by the fact that the amplification systems used differ profoundly. Earlier studies investigated the quorum-sensing system in vivo with a reporter gene transcription/bioluminescence read-out which is much more sensitive than an in vitro AC assay with isolated cell membranes used in the present study (Ng et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on inference comparing different experimental approaches.

claim: The coupling of CqsS to its authentic effector might be more stringent than that attainable in a chimera with an exogenous Rv1625c AC output domain.
source: In addition, the coupling of CqsS to its authentic effector might well be more stringent than that attainable in a chimera with an exogenous Rv1625c AC output domain.
evidence: This is speculation about the efficiency of signal transduction in chimeric proteins.

claim: Use of maltose by E. coli requires activation of the maltose operon via the cAMP/CRP signaling system.
source: Use of maltose by E. coli requires activation of the maltose operon via the cAMP/CRP signaling system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about E. coli metabolism.

claim: Maltose fermentation produces organic acids which are visualized on MacConkey plates by the pH indicator phenol red.
source: Maltose fermentation produces organic acids which are visualized on MacConkey plates by the pH indicator phenol red.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about MacConkey agar plates.

claim: The AC-deficient E. coli cya-99 strain with a high affinity CRP variant cannot metabolize carbohydrates for lack of cAMP.
source: We used the AC-deficient E. coli cya-99 strain with a high affinity CRP variant (Garges and Adhya, 1985). It cannot metabolize carbohydrates for lack of cAMP.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Garges and Adhya, 1985 and established knowledge about the cya-99 strain.

claim: When E. coli cya-99 is grown on MacConkey agar, colonies appear whitish.
source: When grown on MacConkey agar, colonies appear whitish.
evidence: This is experimental observation of bacterial colony phenotype.

claim: The reddish zone along the IPTG filter strip was expanded at the side where CAI-1 was applied, demonstrating CAI-1 stimulated cAMP production in vivo.
source: The reddish zone along the filter strip which is indicative of maltose metabolism was expanded at the side where 10 µl of a 100 µM CAI-1 solution was applied (Figure 4), clearly demonstrating a CAI-1 stimulated cAMP production in vivo.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The monomeric bacterial class III ACs require homodimerization.
source: The monomeric bacterial class III ACs require homodimerization (Linder and Schultz, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Linder and Schultz, 2003.

claim: Bacterial His-kinases of two-component systems are homodimers in which a His-residue of the H-box is phosphorylated either in cis or trans.
source: Similarly, bacterial His-kinases of two-component systems are homodimers in which a His-residue of the H-box is phosphorylated either in cis or trans (Casino et al., 2014; 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Casino et al., 2014; 2009.

claim: The CqsS receptor was connected to known inactive Rv1625c AC point mutants, Rv1625cD300A and Rv1625cR376A.
source: The CqsS receptor was connected to known inactive Rv1625c AC point mutants, Rv1625cD300A and Rv1625cR376A.
evidence: This is experimental data describing the constructs made.

claim: The Rv1625c point mutants D300A and R376A complement each other and the dimer is catalytically active.
source: These point mutants complement each other and the dimer is catalytically active (Guo et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2001.

claim: When CqsS-Rv1625cD300A and CqsS-Rv1625cR376A were jointly expressed, robust AC activity and regulation by CAI-1 was observed.
source: When CqsS-Rv1625cD300A and CqsS-Rv1625cR376A were jointly expressed, robust AC activity and regulation by CAI-1 was observed (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The membrane anchors of CqsS dimerize and allow individually inactive AC domains to form an active, ligand-regulated dimer.
source: This demonstrated that the membrane anchors of CqsS dimerize and allow individually inactive AC domains to form an active, ligand-regulated dimer.
evidence: This is based on inference from the complementation experiment.

claim: The expression product of CqsS-Rv1625cD300A was inactive.
source: Expectedly, the expression product of CqsS-Rv1625cD300A was inactive (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When CqsS-Rv1625cD300A and the full-length Rv1625cR376A were jointly expressed, AC activity was observed, yet CAI-1 did not regulate.
source: First, CqsS-Rv1625cD300A and the full-length Rv1625cR376A were jointly expressed in pETDuet-3. AC activity was observed, yet CAI-1 did not regulate (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When CqsS-Rv1625cD300A and LqsS-Rv1625cR376A were concomitantly expressed, AC activity was restored, yet regulation by CAI-1 was absent.
source: CqsS-Rv1625cD300A and LqsS-Rv1625cR376A were concomitantly expressed. As before, AC activity was restored, yet regulation by CAI-1 was absent (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The membrane anchors in heterodimeric CqsS/Rv1625c and CqsS/LqsS constructs were close enough to enable productive heterodimerization.
source: This indicated that the membrane anchors were close enough to enable productive heterodimerization; however, a regulatory ligand-binding site was absent.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing AC activity but no regulation.

claim: A regulatory ligand-binding site was absent in heterodimeric CqsS/Rv1625c and CqsS/LqsS constructs.
source: This indicated that the membrane anchors were close enough to enable productive heterodimerization; however, a regulatory ligand-binding site was absent.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing no CAI-1 regulation.

claim: One ligand molecule possibly binds at the interface of a receptor homodimer as is the case in the chemotaxis receptors Tsr or Tar or Ni2+-binding in PhoQ.
source: Possibly one ligand molecule binds at the interface of a receptor homodimer as is the case in the chemotaxis receptors Tsr or Tar or Ni2+-binding in PhoQ (Cheung et al., 2008; Gardina and Manson, 1996; Kanchan et al., 2010; Mowbray and Koshland, 1990; Yang et al., 1993).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to analogous systems.

claim: The QS-system of Vibrio controls virulence.
source: The QS-system of Vibrio controls virulence.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Vibrio quorum sensing.

claim: At high cell density, CAI-1 is produced, released and binds to the extracellular CqsS receptor.
source: At high cell density, CAI-1 is produced, released and binds to the extracellular CqsS receptor (Wei et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wei et al., 2012.

claim: CAI-1 binding to CqsS results in reduced production of virulence factors and allows the pathogen to escape from the host, thus spreading disease.
source: In a multistep intracellular process this results in reduced production of virulence factors and allows the pathogen to escape from the host, thus spreading disease (Higgins et al., 2007; Rutherford and Bassler, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Higgins et al., 2007; Rutherford and Bassler, 2012.

claim: CAI-1 may bind within the membrane segments of the CqsS receptor dimer because extracellular loops for ligand binding are absent and because of the lipophilicity of the ligand.
source: Because extracellular loops for ligand binding are absent in CqsS and because of the lipophilicity of the ligand, CAI-1 may bind within the membrane segments of the receptor dimer.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural features and ligand properties.

claim: Membranes pre-treated with 300 nM CAI-1 had an elevated 'basal' AC activity equivalent to the previous 0.3 µM CAI-1 stimulation.
source: Membranes pre-treated with 300 nM CAI-1 had an elevated 'basal' AC activity equivalent to the previous 0.3 µM CAI-1 stimulation (Figure 6, left).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Re-stimulation of membranes pre-treated with 0.3 µM CAI-1 by 0.3 µM CAI-1 failed whereas addition of 10 µM CAI-1 activated to the maximal possible extent.
source: Accordingly, re-stimulation by 0.3 µM CAI-1 failed whereas addition of 10 µM CAI-1 activated to the maximal possible extent.
evidence: This is experimental data from the reversibility experiment.

claim: Membranes which were initially exposed to 10 µM CAI-1 remained almost fully activated and were completely refractory to re-stimulation.
source: Membranes which were initially exposed to 10 µM CAI-1 remained almost fully activated and were completely refractory to re-stimulation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The supernatants of the ultracentrifugation steps of the pre-incubated membranes stimulated naïve membranes according to the previously tested CAI-1 concentrations.
source: The supernatants of the ultracentrifugation steps of the pre-incubated membranes stimulated naïve membranes according to the previously tested CAI-1 concentrations.
evidence: This is experimental data from the reversibility experiment.

claim: Unspecific association of the lipophilic ligand with the membrane or adherence to the reaction vessels was excluded.
source: This excluded unspecific association of the lipophilic ligand with the membrane or adherence to the reaction vessels.
evidence: This is based on inference from the supernatant stimulation experiment.

claim: CAI-1 stimulation was irreversible.
source: Therefore, we can conclude that CAI-1 stimulation was irreversible.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing persistent activation.

claim: CAI-1 stimulation is slightly reminiscent of the biochemistry of rhodopsin in the mammalian eye.
source: This is slightly reminiscent on the biochemistry of rhodopsin in the mammalian eye.
evidence: This is speculation drawing an analogy to rhodopsin.

claim: In rhodopsin, retinal is covalently bound into the membrane-segments of opsin, a GPCR with scant extra-membrane loops.
source: There, retinal is even covalently bound into the membrane-segments of opsin, a GPCR with scant extra-membrane loops.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about rhodopsin structure.

claim: After excitation, rhodopsin receptor regeneration requires ligand removal by an enzymatic process and transport to the retinal pigment epithelium.
source: After excitation receptor regeneration requires ligand removal by an enzymatic process and transport to the retinal pigment epithelium which, notably, contains exclusively adenylate cyclase type VII (Völkel et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Völkel et al., 1996.

claim: The retinal pigment epithelium contains exclusively adenylate cyclase type VII.
source: After excitation receptor regeneration requires ligand removal by an enzymatic process and transport to the retinal pigment epithelium which, notably, contains exclusively adenylate cyclase type VII (Völkel et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Völkel et al., 1996.

claim: The homodimeric catalytic domain of the canonical class IIIa Rv1625c AC was capable to decode the ligand-initiated conformational signal of a 6TM QS-receptor and translate it into a change in AC activity.
source: The above data demonstrated that the homodimeric catalytic domain of the canonical class IIIa Rv1625c AC was capable to decode the ligand-initiated conformational signal of a 6TM QS-receptor and translate it into a change in AC activity.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing ligand-dependent AC regulation.

claim: The functional membrane anchor replacement accompanied by a gain of a novel physiological function suggests that the Rv1625c 6TM anchor actually constitutes an orphan receptor.
source: The functional membrane anchor replacement accompanied by a gain of a novel physiological function suggests that the Rv1625c 6TM anchor actually constitutes an orphan receptor, i.e. receptor without known ligand.
evidence: This is based on inference from the successful functional replacement of membrane anchors.

claim: From the Uniprot Reference Proteomes databank all class III ACs were obtained using the highly conserved catalytic domain for data mining.
source: From the Uniprot Reference Proteomes databank we obtained all class III ACs using the highly conserved catalytic domain for data mining (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the bioinformatic methodology used.

claim: The combined data set comprising a total of 1616 6TM modules was subjected to a cluster analysis using the CLANS software.
source: The combined data set comprising a total of 1616 6TM modules was subjected to a cluster analysis using the CLANS software (Figure 7A; Frickey and Lupas, 2004).
evidence: This describes the bioinformatic methodology and is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Six distinct clusters of 6TM modules were observed, five of which were interconnected to different extents.
source: In total, six distinct clusters were observed, five of which were interconnected to different extents, among them the cluster of QS-receptors (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is data from the cluster analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The clear-cut separation of 6TM modules is surprising and revealing.
source: This clear-cut separation of 6TM modules is surprising and revealing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cluster analysis results.

claim: Transmembrane spanning α-helices have a strong predilection for hydrophobic residues with Leu, Ile, Val, Ala, Gly and Phe comprising two-thirds.
source: Transmembrane spanning α-helices have a strong predilection for hydrophobic residues with Leu, Ile, Val, Ala, Gly and Phe comprising two-thirds (Senes et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Senes et al., 2000.

claim: The unequivocal clustering indicates a differentiated pattern of conserved 6TM variants which is at odds with an assignment of simply an anchoring device.
source: Yet, the unequivocal clustering indicates a differentiated pattern of conserved 6TM variants which is at odds with an assignment of simply an anchoring device.
evidence: This is based on inference from the cluster analysis results.

claim: The diversity of conserved patterned subtypes mirrors a succinct adaptation to particular physiological functions.
source: We propose that the diversity of conserved patterned subtypes mirrors a succinct adaptation to particular physiological functions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cluster analysis results.

claim: By far the majority of 6TM modules were eukaryotic ACs, from the slime mold Dictyostelium, the extant coelacanth up to man.
source: By far the majority of 6TM modules were eukaryotic ACs, from the slime mold Dictyostelium, the extant coelacanth up to man.
evidence: This is data from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The preponderance of eukaryotic sequences is, at least in part, due to the fact that in vertebrates nine distinct membrane-delimited pseudoheterodimeric AC isoforms exist, each with two TM modules, TM1 and TM2.
source: The preponderance of eukaryotic sequences is, at least in part, due to the fact that in vertebrates nine distinct membrane-delimited pseudoheterodimeric AC isoforms exist, each with two TM modules, TM1 and TM2.
evidence: This is based on inference from known AC structure and the dataset composition.

claim: An isolated, unconnected cluster of 30 bacterial class IIIb ACs is characterized by a ferredoxin between the membrane and the catalytic domain.
source: (1) An isolated, unconnected cluster of 30 bacterial class IIIb ACs is characterized by a ferredoxin between the membrane and the catalytic domain.
evidence: This is data from the cluster analysis describing cluster 1.

claim: A representative example of cluster 1 is an AC from Rhodopseudomonas palustris (Uniprot Q132R4) which intracellularly appends to a ferredoxin module.
source: A representative example is an AC from Rhodopseudomonas palustris (Uniprot Q132R4) which intracellularly appends to a ferredoxin module.
evidence: This is data from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The membrane anchors of cluster 1 show sequence similarity to the cytochrome b subunits present in the fumarate reductase/succinate dehydrogenase protein families to an extent that they can be matched by simple BLAST searches.
source: The membrane anchors show sequence similarity to the cytochrome b subunits present in the fumarate reductase/succinate dehydrogenase protein families to an extent that they can be matched by simple BLAST searches.
evidence: This is data from sequence similarity analysis.

claim: The 6TM modules of cluster 1 have four precisely spaced intra-membrane histidine residues which coordinate heme as an electron carrier.
source: These 6TM modules have four precisely spaced intra-membrane histidine residues which coordinate heme as an electron carrier (Einsle et al., 2000; Hederstedt, 1998; Kern et al., 2010a; 2010b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Einsle et al., 2000; Hederstedt, 1998; Kern et al., 2010a; 2010b.

claim: It can confidently be predicted that the AC 6TM anchors of cluster 1 will turn out to contain two heme entities as prosthetic groups.
source: It can confidently be predicted that the AC 6TM anchors of this cluster will turn out to contain two heme entities as prosthetic groups.
evidence: This is speculation based on sequence similarity to heme-containing proteins.

claim: Cluster 2 consists of 118 bacterial class IIIb ACs characterized by a signal-transducing HAMP domain between membrane anchor and catalytic domain.
source: (2) A cluster of 118 bacterial class IIIb ACs is characterized by a signal-transducing HAMP domain between membrane anchor and catalytic domain such as the well-studied mycobacterial AC Rv3645 (Hazelbauer et al., 2008; Hulko et al., 2006; Kanchan et al., 2010; Mondéjar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is data from the cluster analysis describing cluster 2, supported by citations.

claim: Cluster 3 consists of 42 bacterial class IIIb ACs that show partly high local similarity to ACs of cluster 2.
source: (3) A cluster of 42 bacterial class IIIb ACs shows partly high local similarity to ACs of cluster (2) as visualized by the number and intensity of the gray colored connecting lines between both clusters (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is data from the cluster analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: ACs in cluster 3 lack a HAMP domain.
source: Yet, ACs in cluster (3) lack a HAMP domain.
evidence: This is data from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: None of the ACs in cluster 3 has ever been interrogated experimentally.
source: To our knowledge, none of these ACs has ever been interrogated experimentally.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Cluster 4 consists of 35 membrane anchors from bacterial class IIIa ACs as prototypically represented by the mycobacterial AC Rv1625c.
source: (4) A cluster of 35 membrane anchors from bacterial class IIIa ACs as prototypically represented by the mycobacterial AC Rv1625c used here.
evidence: This is data from the cluster analysis describing cluster 4.

claim: Cluster 4 is predominantly connected to the cluster with mammalian TM modules.
source: It is predominantly connected to the cluster with mammalian TM modules.
evidence: This is data from the cluster analysis.

claim: Cluster 5 consists of two tightly connected groups of 677 TM1 and 653 TM2 modules derived from eukaryotic, mostly vertebrate, pseudoheterodimeric class IIIa ACs.
source: (5) Two tightly connected groups are combined here into one cluster of 677 TM1 and 653 TM2 modules which are derived from eukaryotic, mostly vertebrate, pseudoheterodimeric class IIIa ACs.
evidence: This is data from the cluster analysis describing cluster 5.

claim: The difference in the number of TM1 and TM2 units is due to individual sequence divergences of the TM2 domains, database miss-annotations, and problems in the automated prediction of transmembrane spans.
source: The difference in the number of TM1 and TM2 units is due to individual sequence divergences of the TM2 domains, database miss-annotations, and problems in the automated prediction of transmembrane spans.
evidence: This is based on inference from bioinformatic analysis challenges.

claim: Cluster 6 consists of 56 6TM modules corresponding to quorum-sensing receptors of the CqsS type.
source: (6) A cluster of 56 6TM modules corresponds to quorum-sensing receptors of the CqsS type.
evidence: This is data from the cluster analysis describing cluster 6.

claim: The cluster of the eukaryotic TM1 domain was connected to the clusters of the bacterial type IIIa and type IIIb by a large number of pairwise matches, typically covering all six transmembrane spans.
source: The cluster of the eukaryotic TM1 domain (from cluster 5) was connected to the clusters of the bacterial type IIIa (4) and type IIIb (3) by a large number of pairwise matches, typically covering all six transmembrane spans.
evidence: This is data from the cluster analysis.

claim: The CqsS cluster had significantly fewer and only local matches, aligning quorum-sensing sequences specifically to transmembrane spans 1 and 2 of individual eukaryotic AC TM1 sequences and to TM 3, 4 and 5 of the bacterial type IIIa ACs.
source: In contrast, the CqsS cluster had significantly fewer and only local matches, aligning quorum-sensing sequences specifically to transmembrane spans 1 and 2 of individual eukaryotic AC TM1 sequences (all from the bony fish Osteichtyes), and to TM 3, 4 and 5 of the bacterial type IIIa ACs, each at approximately 20–25% identity.
evidence: This is data from the cluster analysis.

claim: The average sequence identity within the clusters themselves is approximately 40%.
source: Notably, the average sequence identity within the clusters themselves is approximately 40%.
evidence: This is data from the sequence analysis.

claim: The observed similarities between CqsS and AC membrane domains may indicate remote homology at the limit of recognition or convergence due to identical structural and functional constraints.
source: Thus, currently we can only speculate whether the observed similarities indicate remote homology at the limit of recognition or convergence due to identical structural and functional constraints.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary relationship between the clusters.

claim: Visual inspection of sequence properties of single TMs indicated a remarkable shortness of α-helices and respective interconnecting loops.
source: Visual inspection of sequence properties of single TMs indicated a remarkable shortness of α-helices and respective interconnecting loops already apparent in the 2D presentations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of sequence data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The loops in 6TM AC anchors are by far shorter than those of comparable sensory proteins, such as mammalian GPCRs with seven TMs, bacterial chemotaxis receptors, His-kinases and ACs with 2 TMs or 4 TMs.
source: Notably, the loops are by far shorter than those of comparable sensory proteins, such as mammalian GPCRs with seven TMs, bacterial chemotaxis receptors, His-kinases and ACs with 2 TMs or 4 TMs such as the chase domain (cyclase/histidine kinases associated sensory extracellular).
evidence: This is based on comparison of structural features across different protein families.

claim: The lengths of the six TM segments and of the five loops were well conserved between orthologues of the same anchor type.
source: The lengths of the six TM segments and of the five loops were well conserved between orthologues of the same anchor type and highly similar between anchors of the bacterial AC classes IIIa and IIIb, eukaryotic TM1, and, most surprisingly, CqsS-like QS-receptors (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is data from the length analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The lengths of TM segments and loops were highly similar between anchors of the bacterial AC classes IIIa and IIIb, eukaryotic TM1, and CqsS-like QS-receptors.
source: The lengths of the six TM segments and of the five loops were well conserved between orthologues of the same anchor type and highly similar between anchors of the bacterial AC classes IIIa and IIIb, eukaryotic TM1, and, most surprisingly, CqsS-like QS-receptors (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is data from the length analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The eukaryotic TM2 anchors, those of the ferredoxin-associated class IIIb, and anchors coupled to a cytosolic HAMP-domain had one or even several elongated loops or α-helices.
source: On the other hand, the eukaryotic TM2 anchors, those of the ferredoxin-associated class IIIb, and anchors coupled to a cytosolic HAMP-domain (class IIIb ACs in cluster 2) had one or even several elongated loops or α-helices (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is data from the length analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The short helices of around 20 residues in the 6TM module design must cross the 30 Å thick lipid bilayer almost orthogonally.
source: The short helices of around 20 residues in this 6TM module design must cross the 30 Å thick lipid bilayer almost orthogonally and the short connecting loops restrict the number of positional permutations foreshadowing a compact packing.
evidence: This is based on inference from structural constraints of membrane proteins.

claim: The short connecting loops restrict the number of positional permutations foreshadowing a compact packing.
source: The short helices of around 20 residues in this 6TM module design must cross the 30 Å thick lipid bilayer almost orthogonally and the short connecting loops restrict the number of positional permutations foreshadowing a compact packing.
evidence: This is based on inference from structural constraints.

claim: The structures of transmembrane domains of eukaryotic AC TM1, the bacterial class IIIa ACs such as Rv1625c, and QS-receptors of the CqsS type can be reasoned to possess overall structural similarities with that of cytochrome b561.
source: Therefore, the structures of transmembrane domains of eukaryotic AC TM1, the bacterial class IIIa ACs such as Rv1625c, and QS-receptors of the CqsS type can be reasoned to possess overall structural similarities with that of cytochrome b561.
evidence: This is based on inference from the similar length parameters and structural constraints.

claim: In 1989 the analysis of the first aa sequence of a mammalian AC suggested that the two membrane anchors might carry a transporter or channel function.
source: In 1989 the analysis of the first aa sequence of a mammalian AC suggested that the two membrane anchors, each consisting of six transmembrane segments, might carry a transporter or channel function (Krupinski et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Krupinski et al., 1989.

claim: To date no function for approximately 40% of a class IIIa AC protein sequence has been identified which goes beyond a mere membrane fixation.
source: Since then, our knowledge concerning the membrane anchors has not advanced; to date no function for approximately 40% of a class IIIa AC protein sequence has been identified which goes beyond a mere membrane fixation.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: This is the first demonstration that a canonical class IIIa AC with a 6TM membrane anchor is directly regulated by a membrane receptor of an identical design with a known ligand.
source: After 26 years we demonstrate for the first time that a canonical class IIIa AC with a 6TM membrane anchor is directly regulated by a membrane receptor of an identical design, yet with a known ligand, the QS-receptor from V. harveyi.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In absence of bacterial G-proteins bacterial class III ACs probably will turn out to be directly regulated via their prominent membrane anchors.
source: In absence of bacterial G-proteins bacterial class III ACs probably will turn out to be directly regulated via their prominent membrane anchors with the above mentioned R. palustris AC as an emerging example.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and the absence of G-proteins in bacteria.

claim: The membrane anchors of the class IIIa bacterial ACs are highly diverged whereas the catalytic domains are conserved.
source: In fact the membrane anchors of the class IIIa bacterial ACs are highly diverged whereas the catalytic domains are conserved (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is data from sequence analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: In bacteria the TM domains have evolved independently and very rapidly relative to the catalytic domains.
source: This suggests that in bacteria the TM domains have evolved independently and very rapidly relative to the catalytic domains.
evidence: This is based on inference from the sequence divergence patterns.

claim: Mutations in upstream regulatory domains mostly are neutral and over time a variety of ligand specificities have evolved by chance mutations.
source: This is in agreement with the general observation that mutations in upstream regulatory domains mostly are neutral and over time a variety of ligand specificities have evolved by chance mutations.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about protein evolution.

claim: Even slightly detrimental mutations in downstream effector domains are not tolerated, thus resulting in sequence and functional conservation.
source: At the same time even slightly detrimental mutations in downstream effector domains are not tolerated, thus resulting in sequence and functional conservation (Schultz and Natarajan, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schultz and Natarajan, 2013.

claim: In such an evolutionary scenario the mechanisms of signal transduction per se remain intact and allow revealing combinatorial diversity.
source: In such an evolutionary scenario the mechanisms of signal transduction per se remain intact and allow revealing combinatorial diversity as demonstrated here (Schultz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schultz et al., 2015 and the experimental data.

claim: In vertebrates the membrane-delimited ACs are regulated indirectly by GPCR activation which intracellularly results in release of Gα proteins.
source: In contrast, in vertebrates the membrane-delimited ACs are regulated indirectly by GPCR activation which intracellularly results in release of Gα proteins.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about vertebrate AC regulation.

claim: The AC membrane bundles of vertebrates are highly conserved in an isoform-specific manner from the coelacanth to man.
source: Because the AC membrane bundles of vertebrates are highly conserved in an isoform-specific manner from the coelacanth to man (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 3 as an example of mammalian AC_I and AC_II subtypes) one can reasonably assume that they have an indispensable physiological function.
evidence: This is data from sequence analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The conserved AC membrane bundles of vertebrates have an indispensable physiological function.
source: Because the AC membrane bundles of vertebrates are highly conserved in an isoform-specific manner from the coelacanth to man (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 3 as an example of mammalian AC_I and AC_II subtypes) one can reasonably assume that they have an indispensable physiological function.
evidence: This is based on inference from evolutionary conservation.

claim: The indispensable physiological function of vertebrate AC membrane bundles could be a particular compartmentalized membrane localization or a hidden receptor function.
source: This could be a particular compartmentalized membrane localization e.g. described in (Crossthwaite et al., 2005) or, in our view more likely and in accordance with our findings an as yet hidden receptor function, as a direct ligand-binding module or in conjunction with an accessory membrane protein that operates as the true sensor.
evidence: This is speculation about possible functions, supported by citation to Crossthwaite et al., 2005.

claim: In vertebrates regulation of intracellular cAMP concentrations may be subject to an interaction between direct, ligand-mediated and indirect GPCR-Gsα-regulated effects.
source: The second alternative would suggest that in vertebrates regulation of intracellular cAMP concentrations is subject to an interaction between direct, ligand-mediated and indirect GPCR-Gsα-regulated effects.
evidence: This is speculation about potential regulatory mechanisms in vertebrates.

claim: A lasting receptor occupation by a ligand during different physiological states might set the responsiveness of mammalian AC isoforms to a transient GPCR-Gsα activation.
source: A lasting receptor occupation by a ligand during different physiological states might well set the responsiveness of mammalian AC isoforms to a transient GPCR-Gsα activation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential regulatory mechanisms.

claim: This would allow that lasting and transient physiological conditions converge via direct and indirect regulation in a central second messenger system, a situation absent in bacteria.
source: This would allow that lasting and transient physiological conditions converge via direct and indirect regulation in a central second messenger system, a situation absent in bacteria.
evidence: This is speculation about potential regulatory mechanisms.

claim: The bacterial AC 6TM anchors can be functionally replaced by the E. coli chemotaxis receptors for serine or aspartate.
source: Recently we demonstrated that we could functionally replace the bacterial AC 6TM anchors by the E. coli chemotaxis receptors for serine or aspartate (Kanchan et al., 2010; Schultz et al., 2015; Winkler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kanchan et al., 2010; Schultz et al., 2015; Winkler et al., 2012.

claim: The results of replacing AC anchors with chemotaxis receptors supported the hypothesis of a receptor function for the AC membrane anchors.
source: By analogy, the results supported the hypothesis of a receptor function for the AC membrane anchors.
evidence: This is based on inference from the cited experiments.

claim: The 2D models of the membrane anchors of Rv1625c and CqsS are similar.
source: The 2D models of the membrane anchors of Rv1625c and CqsS are similar (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1.

claim: The similarity of Rv1625c and CqsS membrane anchors should allow an almost isosteric replacement.
source: This should allow an almost isosteric replacement.
evidence: This is based on inference from structural similarity.

claim: Competent QS-receptor and cyclase chimeras were dependent on the point of linkage.
source: Competent QS-receptor and cyclase chimeras were dependent on the point of linkage indicating that the connecting sites had been evolutionarily predesigned, were conserved and fully operational for signal transduction between functionally differing proteins (Schultz and Natarajan, 2013).
evidence: This is experimental data supported by citation to Schultz and Natarajan, 2013.

claim: The connecting sites between CqsS and Rv1625c had been evolutionarily predesigned, were conserved and fully operational for signal transduction between functionally differing proteins.
source: Competent QS-receptor and cyclase chimeras were dependent on the point of linkage indicating that the connecting sites had been evolutionarily predesigned, were conserved and fully operational for signal transduction between functionally differing proteins (Schultz and Natarajan, 2013).
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data, supported by citation.

claim: The dependence on linkage point implicitly supports the prediction that the 6TM anchors of such ACs have a receptor function for which stimuli have yet to be identified.
source: Implicitly this supports the prediction that the 6TM anchors of such ACs have a receptor function for which stimuli have yet to be identified.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Because the ligands for CqsS and LqsS are known, the direct regulation of AC activity is no real surprise.
source: Because the ligands for CqsS and LqsS are known, the direct regulation of AC activity then is no real surprise.
evidence: This is based on inference from the availability of known ligands.

claim: Mixing and matching TM domains of eukaryotic AC is impossible without loss of activity.
source: First mixing and matching TM domains of eukaryotic AC is impossible without loss of activity (Seebacher et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seebacher et al., 2001.

claim: The cluster analysis visualizes similarities between individual pairs of CqsS receptor type modules and membrane anchors from class IIIa ACs.
source: Second, the cluster analysis visualizes similarities between individual pairs of CqsS receptor type modules and membrane anchors from class IIIa ACs.
evidence: This is data from the cluster analysis.

claim: The cluster analysis supports the hypothesis that the membrane anchors of class III ACs, bacterial and mammalian alike have a function beyond membrane fixation.
source: Thus it supports the hypothesis that the membrane anchors of class III ACs, bacterial and mammalian alike have a function beyond membrane fixation.
evidence: This is based on inference from the cluster analysis results.

claim: Cluster 1 demonstrates that comparable transmembrane architectures can result in significantly different sequence patterns notwithstanding the similar amino acid composition commonly shared by all membrane domains.
source: In this context cluster (1), which is unrelated to all other clusters, is particularly interesting. It demonstrates that comparable transmembrane architectures can result in significantly different sequence patterns notwithstanding the similar amino acid composition commonly shared by all membrane domains.
evidence: This is based on inference from the cluster analysis results.

claim: Currently, it is impossible to speculate about or even predict the nature of ligands for the 6TM AC modules examined.
source: Currently, it is impossible to speculate about or even predict the nature of ligands for the 6TM AC modules examined here.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current knowledge.

claim: Ligands for 6TM AC modules might be expected to be closely associated with the intra-membrane space as extra-membranous loops for ligand-binding are noticeably absent.
source: One might expect, however, that they will be closely associated with the intra-membrane space as extra-membranous loops for ligand-binding are noticeably absent in this type of 6TM bundles.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural features of the 6TM modules.
